analysis.one_liner: Makes the 2003 investment tax cuts on capital gains and dividends permanent instead of expiring.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee from June 2003 until the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2003 tax law cut the tax rates on capital gains and stock dividends, but only temporarily — the cuts were scheduled to expire, which kept the law's official price tag lower. This bill would have removed the expiration date, making those lower rates permanent. Because investment income goes mostly to higher-income households, the direct savings would have gone mainly to them, with the cost showing up as federal revenue lost over time. The bill was sent to the Ways and Means Committee and never moved again; it received no hearing, no vote, and died when the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Households with capital gains and dividend income — which skew heavily toward the wealthiest Americans — would pay lower taxes on investment income permanently, with no scheduled increase. Financial services firms and asset managers would also benefit from stronger incentives to hold and trade taxed-advantaged investments. The broader public gains nothing direct; at most, supporters argue lower taxes on investment encourage economic growth, a claim the bill's record does not test.

how_it_helps.text: It removes the expiration date the 2003 law placed on its investment tax provisions, so investors would not face a scheduled tax increase on capital gains and dividends.
The bill changes the sunset provision of the 2003 law so that the reduced rates no longer terminate automatically, converting a temporary cut into a permanent feature of the tax code.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury bears the cost of the permanently lower rates, meaning either larger deficits or higher taxes or lower spending elsewhere to make up the difference. Since the direct savings go to households with investment income while the lost revenue must be recovered from everyone, the burden of paying for it falls broadly, including on people who own few or no stocks.

drawbacks.text: The bill had no revenue offset: making the investment tax cuts permanent would reduce federal revenue for as long as they stayed in effect, adding to deficits or forcing other taxes or spending to make up the difference.

The benefits were concentrated: because capital gains and dividend income flows disproportionately to higher-income households, the direct tax savings would go overwhelmingly to those already at the top, while the indirect costs of the lost revenue fall on everyone.

Supporters of the original 2003 law built in the expiration date deliberately, to hold down its official cost estimate; making the cuts permanent removes that limit, which is exactly what budget scorekeepers warned about.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a real benefit to a specific group: investors and wealthy households would keep lower tax rates on capital gains and dividends beyond their scheduled expiration. The cost was broader and less visible: every dollar of revenue not collected adds to deficits or must be made up by other taxes, and the benefit flowed overwhelmingly to households that already own substantial assets, so the gains and costs were unevenly distributed. The bill made no attempt to pair the permanence with revenue offsets, which is the strongest good-faith objection to it. Its death in committee means none of this was ever weighed in a floor vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 108th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 26, 2003 and referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
No further action was ever recorded: the committee never reported the bill and it never reached the House floor before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal Treasury, and taxpayers generally, are better off because the investment tax cuts were not made permanent; the expiration dates in the 2003 law remained in effect, and wealthy households did not get the permanent rate lock this bill offered.

for.name: Rep. Phil English
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 26, 2003 to make the 2003 investment tax cuts permanent.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 26, 2003 and never reported it out; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever recorded before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 26 cosponsors, along with the sponsor, were Republicans, but the bill never reached a vote, so no one's position was ever tested on the record.

industries.note: Investors with large capital gains and dividend income would keep permanently lower tax rates on that income, the main direct benefit of the bill. Because this income is concentrated among the wealthiest households, so is the benefit.

Permanently lower tax rates on investment income make taxed-advantaged investing more attractive, supporting demand for brokerage, fund, and advisory services. The benefit to the industry is indirect but durable.
